To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
third-degree price discrimination can increase aggregate consumer surplus and that the conditions under which this is the case are quite reasonable.

1) the aggregate consumer surplus is higher when a monopolist engages in third-degree price discrimination than when it charges a uniform price, 2) the consumer surplus is higher under price discrimination if the pass-through coefficient is sufficiently high, and 3) the consumer surplus can be higher with price discrimination even when the pass-through coefficient and the uniform price are low.

(i) third-degree price discrimination is likely to reduce consumer surplus, (ii) the reduction can be small, (iii) the reduction is larger when the price elasticities are more similar (i.e. the price elasticities of demand are closer to each other) and (iv) the reduction is also larger when the pass-through coefficients are more similar.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of third-degree price discrimination, in particular, the effect on consumer surplus.
the welfare implications of price discrimination.
the welfare effects of third degree price discrimination in the context of monopolistic competition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of price discrimination on aggregate surplus are ambiguous.
the effects on aggregate consumer surplus of monopoly price discrimination are ambiguous.
third-degree price discrimination can increase or decrease aggregate consumer surplus.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
third degree price discrimination is not necessarily bad for consumers, and that the effect on consumer surplus is ambiguous in general.
price discrimination is likely to reduce aggregate consumer surplus, but that it can raise surplus under some circumstances.
the effect of discrimination on surplus is ambiguous, but that it is likely to increase surplus if the pass-through coefficient is high in the market with high price elasticity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effect of price discrimination on aggregate surplus is ambiguous.
the welfare effects of third-degree price discrimination are ambiguous.
the effects of price discrimination are not necessarily negative for consumer surplus.
